readerTitle: Why a one-page memo takes longer to write, and saves more time
caseNote: 가상 사례 (리모델링 회사, B2B 시설관리 업체) + 실제 관찰 (Pascal의 문장, Amazon의 6페이지 메모) · 시간 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 한 페이지 제한은 읽는 사람을 위한 배려이기 전에, 쓰는 사람이 무엇이 중요한지 고르게 만드는 사고 도구다.
misconception: 한 페이지 메모는 긴 문서를 줄여 쓴 요약본이고, 길고 자세할수록 더 철저한 문서다.

sources.text: Blaise Pascal, Lettres provinciales (1657), 16th letter: "I have made this longer than usual because I have not had time to make it shorter."
Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2017 Letter to Shareholders (six-page narrative memos)
모든 시간 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 시간 계산(가상): 긴 문서 = 작성 2시간 + 읽기 6명×30분 3시간 + 회의 7명×1시간 7시간 = 12시간. 한 페이지 = 작성 4시간 + 읽기 6명×5분 0.5시간 + 회의 7명×30분 3.5시간 = 8시간. 차이 4시간(약 33% 감소).
Pascal 문장은 『시골 친구에게 보내는 편지』 16번째 편지(1657)에 나옵니다. 영어 번역 표현은 판본마다 조금 다르므로 카드에는 의역 형태로 적었습니다. 게시 전 번역 문구를 확인하세요.
Amazon이 회의에서 파워포인트 대신 6페이지 서술형 메모를 쓴다는 내용은 Bezos의 2017년 주주서한에 나옵니다. 게시 전 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why a one-page memo takes longer to write, and saves more time
body: A ten-page proposal takes two hours to write. A one-page version of the same idea takes four.
The short one costs twice as much to produce. Yet across the whole team, it usually saves hours, and it gets a decision made.

image.label: A thick stack of pages next to a single sheet
image.brief: 책상 위에 두꺼운 서류 더미와 종이 한 장이 나란히 놓여 있음. 종이 한 장 옆에는 더 큰 모래시계, 서류 더미 옆에는 작은 모래시계. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your project manager sends ten pages.
body: You co-own a home renovation company. Your project manager wants to switch from hourly billing to fixed-price quotes. She sends the three partners a ten-page proposal.
Everyone is busy, and the partners' meeting is next week. What do you ask her for?

options.text: Keep the ten pages, but add a summary at the top
options.feedback: Readers save time, but she never had to choose what matters most. The weak spots stay buried on page seven.

options.text: One page: the decision, why, the costs and risks, what's needed. Details go in an appendix
options.feedback: It costs her more effort up front. In return, she has to commit to a recommendation, and the partners can judge it in minutes.

options.text: Skip the document and talk it through at the meeting
options.feedback: Faster for her, but nobody arrives having thought it through. The loudest partner tends to win, and there's no record of why you decided.

cards.title: Count everyone's hours, not just the writer's.
body: Six readers and a seven-person meeting. The writer spends **twice as long**, and the team spends a third less time overall.

breakdown.label: Reading
breakdown.detail: 6 readers: 30 min each vs 5 min each

breakdown.label: Total team time
breakdown.detail: The extra writing pays for itself

cards.title: The one-page memo
body: A **one-page memo** is a decision document with a hard length limit and a fixed shape: what we're deciding, what I recommend, why, what it costs, what could go wrong, and what happens next.
Everything else goes in an appendix that readers can open if they want.
The limit isn't mainly for the reader. It's for the writer. When only a few things fit, you have to decide which few things matter.

image.label: A single page divided into six labeled boxes
image.brief: 종이 한 장을 여섯 칸으로 나눈 인포그래픽. 칸마다 "Decision", "Recommendation", "Why", "Cost", "Risks", "Next step" 라벨. 종이 뒤로 "Appendix"라고 적힌 얇은 서류가 살짝 보임.

cards.title: Cutting is where the thinking happens.
body: The philosopher Blaise Pascal once apologized for a long letter, saying he hadn't had time to make it shorter. Cutting is hard because each cut is a judgment call. A one-page limit forces three of them:
list: **Pick one recommendation.** No room to list five options and hope someone chooses.
**Name the top reasons.** Two or three, not twelve.
**Face the main risk.** Hiding it would take space you don't have.
cards.callout: If you can't fill the page clearly, you may not be ready to decide yet.
cards.softwareNote: A product team asking to rebuild a feature can write one page: the problem in numbers, the proposed fix, the engineering weeks it needs, and what gets delayed. The roadmap details go in the appendix.

cards.title: Short is not the same as simple.
body: Some decisions really are complex. Amazon, for example, asks for longer six-page narrative memos for big meetings. The principle is the same: a fixed limit and full sentences, not a slide of bullet points.

The bigger danger is cutting the wrong things. A one-page memo that drops the risks and costs to stay upbeat is short and misleading. Trim background and history first, never the parts that could change the answer.

cards.title: Now it's a facilities contract.
body: You run a commercial cleaning firm. You want a client's operations director to expand your contract to two more buildings at a higher monthly fee. Your draft runs to three pages.
What do you cut to fit one page?

options.text: Cut the section on transition risks so the pitch stays positive
options.feedback: It reads better, but the director will spot the gap and trust the rest less. The risks are what she needs most to say yes.

options.text: Move the account history and task-by-task checklist to an appendix
options.feedback: The page keeps the ask, the price, the reasons and the risks. She loses nothing she needs, and the detail is still there if she wants it.

options.text: Shrink the font and margins until all three pages fit
options.feedback: Technically one page, but you've skipped the choosing. It's as slow to read as before, and the ask is still hard to find.

cards.title: A one-page limit makes you decide what matters.
body: The page limit costs the writer more time and saves everyone else much more. Above all, it forces a clear recommendation, honest risks and a next step.
**Try it today:** take one proposal you're working on. Write it on a single page under six headings: decision, recommendation, why, cost, risks, next step. Notice what you had to leave out.
